newsitem.title: POLAND: PENSION REFORM TO GET PLN 42 BLN FROM POLISH SALES.
newsitem.headline: PENSION REFORM TO GET PLN 42 BLN FROM POLISH SALES.

text.p: Poland's government estimates it will spend at least 42 billion zlotys in revenues from the privatisation of state firms to finance its planned social security reform, a deputy treasury minister said on Tuesday.

"According to 1995 estimates, assets suitable for sell-offs have a book value of 144.2 billion zlotys...Out of this sum, roughly 42 billion could support the social security system reform," Ewa Freyberg told a news briefing.
She said these sums were part of a policy document called "Privatisation outlines until the year 2000," approved by the government on Tuesday and now due to go to parliament for discussion.

The government earlier said the reform, which provides for creating new independent pension funds, would require an additional budgetary subsidy amounting to one percent of gross domestic product annually for the next 20 years.

The government plans to generate the necessary funds by public offerings of stakes in those companies with the best financial results and by issuing bonds convertible into shares of some of these firms.

The reform of the ailing social security system would be launched in 1999 if parliament approves several relevant bills, now being discussed by lower house committees, before general elections due around September.
Freyberg said that under the government's privatisation plans only sea and air ports, most road infrastructure, railways and the power grid would eventually remain state-owned.

She also said another eight billion zlotys in revenues from privatisation would be earmarked to compensate public sector workers and pensioners for overdue pay rises, which under a court ruling they should have been given in the early 1990s.
Another seven billion zlotys would be spent to compensate former owners for property confiscated by communist authorities after World War Two and which cannot be returned in kind.

The government wants the owners, public sector workers and pensioners to receive coupons, with which they will be able to pay for shares of companies undergoing privatisation and for other selected state-owned assets.
The bills on the coupons are currently being debated by parliamentary committees, which are delaying their passage.
